# Bizkit

<p class="sx-lede">If a story about a company is memorable, the economics behind it can be too.</p>

Bizkit is a blog I founded and write. Each post starts with something that really happened, such as a bank collapse, a company splitting in two or a banknote being withdrawn, and uses it to explain one idea in business or economics without jargon. Every post appears in six languages, so a student does not need English to read it.

<p class="sx-label">Why it began</p>

## Students meet economics as definitions before they have a reason to care

Elasticity, adverse selection and opportunity cost usually arrive as terms to memorise. I came to economics the other way round: through decisions I could already see, like why a company changed its price or why two firms valued the same deal differently. Bizkit puts the story first and the concept second.

Science and programming have plenty written for young readers; how businesses and economies work has very little, and almost none of it outside English. That is why every post is published in five languages besides English.
:::

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">How a post is made</p>

## One real event, one idea, six languages

::: {.sx-two}

::: {}
I pick an event from the news, find the economic idea that explains why it turned out the way it did, and write the post around the question a curious reader would ask. If I cannot explain an idea without leaning on its textbook definition, I take that as a sign I do not understand it well enough yet.

The translations into Hindi, Kannada, Tamil, Telugu and German are machine-generated, and the header images are made with AI. The site is built with Quarto and published as a static website, with a WhatsApp channel for new posts.
:::

<ol class="sx-flow" aria-label="How a Bizkit post is made">
<li><b>A real event</b><span>A company, market or policy decision in the news</span></li>
<li><b>The surprising detail</b><span>What makes the outcome worth explaining</span></li>
<li><b>The idea</b><span>The economic concept that makes it make sense</span></li>
<li><b>Write and revise</b><span>Plain language, no jargon</span></li>
<li><b>Translate and publish</b><span>Five more languages; shared on the WhatsApp channel</span></li>
</ol>

:::
:::

<p class="sx-label">Where it comes from</p>

## An engineering family, and a different choice

Engineering runs through my family for generations, and I was born on the birthday of Sir M. Visvesvaraya, one of India's most celebrated engineers. I became fascinated by economics instead: not a rejection of the systems thinking I grew up with, but a decision to apply it to people, incentives, firms and markets.

Writing changed how I think. A sentence that feels awkward often means the argument underneath is still unclear, and writing slowly enough makes my assumptions visible.

<blockquote class="sx-pull">
<p>If I extended it today, what would change?</p>
<p>I would make the reader more active: short decisions, interactive cases or simulations in which the idea emerges from a choice rather than an explanation. I specifically like how <a href="https://yadayadayadaecon.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Yada Yada Yada Econ</a>, <a href="https://economicsoftheoffice.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Economics of the Office</a> and <a href="https://www.bazinganomics.com/bazinganomics//time-is-too-valuable" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Bazinganomics</a> have made economics fun. I wonder what a Bazinganomics version of Bizkit would look like.</p>
</blockquote>
:::
